name: ODK
project_description: SDG1: IFRC uses ODK to monitor cash assistance to 1.6M foreigners in Türkiye SDG2: WFP uses ODK to provide actionable food security assessments. SDG3: WHO uses ODK to collect millions of data points for disease surveillance. SDG4: Honduras uses ODK to ensure the education of millions of students. SDG6: Red Cross uses ODK to improve the efficiency of humanitarian action. SDG7: Guyana uses ODK to ensure operational efficiency of its power grid. SDG8: FINCA uses ODK to measure household consumption and job creation. SDG13: Sierra Leone uses ODK to help plant millions of trees and create jobs. SDG14: Australia uses ODK to guide the conservation of flatback turtles. SDG15: Jane Goodall Institute uses ODK to track the health of ape habitat. SDG16: The Carter Center uses ODK to assess the fairness of elections.

name: MOSIP
project_description: SDG1 (End poverty in all forms everywhere): MOSIP focusses on ending poverty in all forms by facilitating implementation of appropriate social protection programs (1.3) and enabling financial inclusion and access to financial services (1.4). SDG2 (Zero Hunger): MOSIP focusses on ending hunger and achieving food security by enabling access to food to all, particularly the poor and vulnerable (2.1) through social assistance, and facilitating access to financial services by the farmers (2.3). SDG3 (Good Health and Well Being): MOSIP contributes to good health and well-being by establishing ID systems that help in efficient targeting and service delivery which are paramount to achieving the goals of health-related strategies, schemes and programs (3.7). MOSIP also enables financial inclusion and, consequently, helps reduce finance risk related to household expenditures on health (3.8). SDG4 (Quality Education): MOSIP enables the process of service delivery which assists policies and programs that further literacy, equitable primary and secondary education and affordable education. SDG5 (Gender Equity): MOSIP assists women empowerment through an equitable infrastructure that advance targeted interventions, greater access to financial services, and economic empowerment through specifically tailored programs. SDG8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth): MOSIP promotes sustained inclusive economic growth. MOSIP facilitates equitable access to banking, insurance, and financial services which enable formalization of the economy. It also furthers better targeting of beneficiaries of various government programs, switching to direct benefit transfers wherever possible and brings in resource efficiency at the national level. SDG9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure): MOSIP enables access to financial services and credit to MSMEs. The establishment of an ID system also creates resilient infrastructure that can significantly alleviate Government response during shocks to the country such as disasters, pandemic, economic downturn, etc. MOSIP is being adopted - in various stages - in 9 African countries. SDG10 (Reduced Inequalities): MOSIP helps countries set up foundational ID systems - which aid in the political, economic and civil inclusion of ID-holders into the country (10.2); MOSIP enables efficient implementations of the policies for social protection and equality (10.4); MOSIP framework can provide a common infrastructure for cross-border identification, facilitating seamless migration. (10.7) SDG16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions): Modular Open Source Identity Platform (MOSIP) provides an open-source modular cost-free platform for countries to adopt and provide a legal foundational ID (16.9). Additionally, the establishment of an ID system in the country also strengthens the institutions of the country such as the legislature, social service delivery, financial ecosystem, etc. Thus, MOSIP contributes to reducing corruption and bribery, and building transparent institutions through the elimination of discretionary layers, enabling of direct benefit transfers, and use of digital authentication (16.5).

name: CKAN
project_description: While CKAN is used by many different organizations tackling many different challenges related to the SDGs, it is specially used to help attain SDG 16 (Promote just, peaceful, and inclusive societies). Perhaps the target most contributes to is 16.10 (Ensure public access to information and protect fundamental freedoms) by providing a free, community-led tool for official institutions to publish their data, which is easy to use for users and provides capabilities for advanced users to monitor and explore the datasets. Being widely used by government and civil society institutions to publish open data, it also helps attain among others target 16.6 (Develop effective, accountable, and transparent institutions) by helping publish data about official budgets, expenditures, declared interests etc, allowing citizens to hold institutions accountable. Other examples where CKAN helps meet the targets of the SDGs include CKAN being used by UNHCR to centralize and standardize refugee-related data, helping with target 10.7 (Facilitating orderly, safe, regular, and responsible migration and mobility of people), and by UNOCHA to host humanitarian data, as well as by several other non-profit organizations working on tackling inequalities around the world (SDG1, SDG10). It is also trusted by many government institutions to publish data that is critical for transparency, accountability and that promotes economic growth (SDG11, SDG8, SDG16). Other organizations like Energinet in Denmark use CKAN to publish energy-related data (SDG7).

name: OpenG2P
project_description: OpenG2P helps advance a number of SDGs by ensuring that low income people receive digital cash transfers from governments or humanitarian agencies. Chiefly, OpenG2P helps countries achieve SDG Target 1.3 by aiding the implementation of nationally appropriate social protection systems and increased coverage of the poor and the vulnerable. Governments and humanitarian agencies can use the OpenG2P platform to register, enrol, manage and send monetary or in-kind support to beneficiaries of their social protection programs (SDG1: End Poverty in all its forms everywhere; SDG2: Zero Hunger). These can be programs which involve sending cash support to lift people out of poverty or food rations to ensure sufficient meals for low income families. OpenG2P can also be used to manage beneficiaries in a health program such as providing cash support to pregnant and lactating women to ensure sufficient nutrition for the mother and child (SDG3: Good Health and Well-Being). It is currently being used in the Philippines to send digitally verifiable vouchers to beneficiaries seeking medical assistance. In the education sector, OpenG2P may be used to disburse scholarships to students, performance-based cash incentives to schools, cash support to families conditional on school attendance of children, all of which are aimed at achieving quality education (SDG4: Quality Education). Similarly, OpenG2P can be used to deliver a host of programs targeted towards women, including health, livelihood, training and education and financial inclusion (SDG5: Gender Equity). Livelihood related programs such as providing cash support to individuals to start small businesses can also benefit from OpenG2P (SDG8: Decent Work and Economic Growth) OpenG2P also serves towards reducing inequalities (SDG10: Reduced Inequalities) by enabling the socio-economic inclusion of the bottom 40% of the population. OpenG2P helps in tracking public expenditure for social development, thereby enabling accountability and transparency in government institutions (SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). Finally, OpenG2P furthers SDG 17: Partnerships for the goals by mobilizing the domestic technology ecosystem of a country, engaging in capacity building and multi-stakeholder partnerships to help a country achieve its goals.

name: AGROVOC Multilingual Thesaurus
project_description: AGROVOC facilitates the exchange and consolidation of knowledge, information, and data in the domains covered by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Consistent use of relevant concepts to index data and resources across repositories and institutions is essential to monitor progress on the SDGs: in the case of AGROVOC, particularly the SDGs that have indicators for which FAO is the custodian UN agency. FAO is the custodian UN agency for 21 indicators and is a contributing agency to 5 more, spanning SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14, and 15. Not only does AGROVOC cover all domains related to the SDGs for whose indicators FAO is custodian, but it also includes a dedicated concept for the SDGs and individual sub-concepts for each SDG, with official definitions (https://agrovoc.fao.org/browse/agrovoc/en/page/?uri=http%3A%2F%2Faims.fao.org%2Faos%2Fagrovoc%2Fc_013b16cd). This helps information and data managers correctly classify resources against the SDGs, and researchers and the general public easily find and browse SDG-related resources and data. AGROVOC is used to index content and data in many information systems relevant to SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14, and 15: library catalogs of agriculture/fisheries/nutrition/land research institutions and Ministries, repositories of the CGIAR centers, the FAO AGRIS database and various other FAO resources. Being a resource managed in partnership with several institutions all over the world, and being coordinated by FAO under the Partnerships and UN Collaboration Division, AGROVOC is particularly relevant to SDG 17.

name: OpenFisca
project_description: - 1: No Poverty OpenFisca makes social and fiscal legislation executable. One of the most common use cases of the resulting API is for government agencies and NGOs to deploy simulators enabling citizens to assess which benefits they are entitled to, allowing them to obtain the social support they should get but too often don't because of lack of information and actionability. Examples: https://www.mesdroitssociaux.gouv.fr (France), https://oecd-opsi.org/innovations/rac-legal-eligibility/ (New Zealand), https://ajuntament.barcelona.cat/lesmevesajudes/ (Spain), https://www.service.nsw.gov.au/campaign/savings-finder (Australia). Impact assessment in France: https://blog.beta.gouv.fr/general/2019/11/18/mes-aides-metriques/; https://blog.beta.gouv.fr/dinsic/2017/05/03/mes-aides-datascience-public/. OpenFisca also improves personal finance and budgeting ability, by enabling any service provider or assistant to compute personal financial obligations and entitlements and predict their evolution across potential life events. Examples: https://pa-comp.firebaseapp.com/ ; https://www.benefitme.nz/ ; https://betagouv.github.io/mes-aides-changent/graphique/?source=/mes-aides-changent/static/celibataire_handicap.json - 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth By making social and fiscal legislation executable, OpenFisca empowers individuals and businesses to assess their best employment opportunities, by removing the guesswork in computing exact income after tax and total cost to the employer. It also eases the creation and expansion of businesses in full respect of the law, by clarifying how regulatory constraints apply specifically to a given context. Examples: https://www.fairtrading.nsw.gov.au/community-gaming/community-gaming-regulation-check/ (context: https://www.digital.nsw.gov.au/article/an-australian-first-nsw-translating-rules-as-code-to-make-compliance-easy) ; https://www.simucrea.fr. - 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure Beyond all the examples listed in other points, that demonstrate how OpenFisca enables innovation and is the central part of an upcoming critical digital infrastructure, APIs based on OpenFisca can model many types of legislation, including niche ones, enabling lawmakers, regulators, and businesses to share a common view of their entitlements and duties and to discuss potential evolutions. Examples: Mining taxes in France are modeled in https://github.com/openfisca/openfisca-france-fiscalite-miniere; the Australian Energy Saving Scheme is modeled in https://www.codeforaustralia.org/case-studies/dpie-rules-as-code, and its National Building Code is being prototyped in a similar fashion. - 10: Reduced Inequalities (within and between countries) OpenFisca supports citizens in assessing their benefits, thus improving access to social safety nets designed for reducing inequalities (cf. SDG1). Beyond that aspect, by consolidating historical legislative data and enabling large-scale, population-wide simulations, OpenFisca enables economists, researchers, NGOs, and lawmakers to assess the impact of existing schemes and potential reforms, improving the understanding of policies impact on inequality and accelerating the delivery of policies to reduce it effectively. Examples: The French Institut des Politiques Publiques measured the impact of 5 years of consolidated fiscal reforms on wealth distribution, and was able to reach that level of precision thanks to OpenFisca: https://www.ipp.eu/en/publication/february-2020-budget-2020-what-effects-on-households/; https://budget.ipp.eu; https://policyengine.org/uk/blog/2023-01-12-from-idea-to-impact-scoring-a-policy-reform-on-the-new-policyengine-uk With growing OpenFisca adoption, cross-country comparison of implementations of similar policies becomes possible: with a simple mapping of the name of each policy in their respective OpenFisca model, researchers can run simulations over multiple years and populations and compare the results of each policy, enabling identification of the most effective ones. An upcoming European Union-funded Multi-Country Project also considers modeling international business rules and taxation, enabling identification and correction of policies that place an undue burden on individuals and businesses operating across countries. - 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities OpenFisca makes social and fiscal legislation executable (see SDG1). Its technical architecture is designed to allow local governments to complete national regulations with their specific rules, empowering regions, cities, and communities to build and improve their own schemes toward inclusion while taking into account the existing laws in which they operate. Examples: the cities of Paris and Brest use OpenFisca to deliver personalized information to residents on their entitlement to local benefits, including mobility and childcare support; Strasbourg used OpenFisca to design the reform of its school canteen scheme, enabling more pupils to access good food at a fair price. OpenFisca can also enable public bodies whose budget is determined based on computable rules to calculate it autonomously and make it publicly auditable. Examples: the French local government's budgets provided by the State are usually calculated in the second quarter of each year, while data to calculate their allotment is available at the beginning of the year, resulting in unnecessary delays for local decision-makers. The app “Dotations Locales” enables cities and residents to calculate that budget earlier and plan accordingly: https://leximpact.an.fr/dotations. - 13: Climate Action OpenFisca enables modeling any sort of legislation that contains a computational part. Carbon emission quotas could thus be modeled, improving their understandability and actionability. Just like with budgetary reforms (see SDG10), assessing the impact of climate-related legislation and ways to make it more effective would be significantly easier, cheaper, and more complete with the consolidated models that take into account interaction with other parts of law, like what OpenFisca delivers. Examples: French benefits for improved housing insulation are made more discoverable to citizens, and the eligibility to the Australian Energy Saving Scheme is made discoverable at https://www.nabers.gov.au/rating-tools/our-calculators/nsw-esc-estimator, enabling a much stronger and faster uptake of this policy (context: https://www.codeforaustralia.org/case-studies/dpie-rules-as-code). - 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions In most democratic countries, the executive branch has both abilities to propose legislation and is uniquely equipped to assess its impact through direct access to the administration, putting the legislative branch in a situation where it hardly has the resources to double-check effectively the impact assessments or to properly assess the impact of its own legislative proposals. The exact same asymmetry prevents many civil society proposals for reforms to reach democratic arenas. The models provided by OpenFisca enable lawmakers and NGOs to discuss and design potential reforms on an objective basis, at a very low cost, and with high accuracy, and to provide citizens with replicable, auditable assessments. Examples: the French Parliament (Assemblée Nationale) provides all Members of Parliament with LexImpact, a tool designed for reform assessment; it also has a public instance enabling any citizen to design their own reforms: https://leximpact.an.fr; PolicyEngine enables reform design for both UK and US legislation: https://policyengine.org/. See also SDG11 for local institutions strengthening. - 17: Partnerships for the Goals Beyond technical aspects, OpenFisca’s specificity in the field of rules engine is its deeply collaborative nature. It is a digital common: both the core engine and the country models are created by a multitude of contributors. The rules and tooling that have progressively emerged to support such collaboration and its growth both enable and depend on active contributions by all actors: public administrations who are in charge of a specific aspect of legislation or regulation, researchers who can add historical depth to the data and analyze the resulting models, civil society who can audit and leverage the calculations; all of this in several countries, leading to a more robust shared core set of tools. This open-source, commons-based approach is enforced with reciprocity licenses and usage charters, and pushes all these actors to create new alliances and collaboration approaches based on shared goals that are embodied in a piece of software available to everyone. See https://oecd-opsi.org/publications/cracking-the-code/ and how OpenFisca's instant messaging system gathers a community of 300+ practitioners from all around the world, ranging from French administrations to American think tanks to Pakistani volunteers, all learning from each other and replicating experiments.

name: OpenStreetMap
project_description: OpenStreetMap (OSM) provides an essential infrastructure and boundary base layer below the overlaid data added by the SDG cartographers. Any aspect of any SDG 1 - 17 that can be mapped can make use of resources provided by OpenStreetMap and most of them currently already use OSM data. Outside of the SDG programme itself, global health organisations like the UN, MSF, ICRC, World Food Programme, and World Bank use countless maps, in many cases these maps are based directly on OSM data. Academics and researchers working in countless fields use OSM data for spatial representation and analysis.

name: Rights Tracker
project_description: We produce country scores for five economic and social rights. These are the rights to education (SDG4), food (SDG2), health (SDG3), housing (SDG6) and work and social assistance (SDG1, SDG8). These scores tell us how well countries are using their available resources to make sure their people can enjoy each of these rights to the maximum extent possible given that country's level of income. Countries with well-functioning governments and effective public sectors perform better, and countries with high levels of corruption or inequality generally perform worse (hence SDG10). Many of the SDG indicators also feed into the Rights Tracker scores. However, unlike the SDGs, our scores are benchmarked according to each country's level of resources. This avoids the income bias problem that is inherent in the SDGs. (i.e. higher income countries generally perform better on most SDG indicators). This is very important as it has been documented (e.g. by the World Bank) that ESG investment strategies that use the SDGs (and simliar) as indicators of development, skew investment away from lower income countries towards higher income countries. Our award-winning methodology avoids this problem. Using a different methodology, we also produce country scores for eight civil and political rights. These relate closely to SDG16 and provide additional metrics not already captured by the SDG16 targets.

name: AgriTech Observatory
project_description: SDG2- AgriTech Observatory serves as a knowledge hub for promoting digital agriculture innovations and policy development, thus enabling practical implementation of these technologies to increase agricultural efficiency and sustainability. SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure – The platform encourages the adoption of digital technologies, helping to modernize agricultural practices, support innovation, and strengthen infrastructure for sustainable agriculture. SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production – Digital tools, among those highlighted in the platform, can optimize resource use, minimize waste, and promote sustainable practices. SDG 13: Climate Action – By tracking and promoting climate-smart agricultural practices, the Observatory contributes to adaptation and mitigation strategies, helping farmers address climate change impacts. SDG 15: Life on Land – Sustainable digital agriculture practices can improve soil health, biodiversity, and ecosystem conservation, supporting the protection and restoration of terrestrial ecosystems. SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals – The Observatory is built upon collaboration with several institutions, including JengaLab, the Central European University, the American University of Central Asia, the Georgian Farmers Association, and the Digital AgriHub.

name: X-Road®
project_description: In order to ensure more universal and affordable access to digital services for the population of developing countries, X-Road has been introduced in multiple projects around the world. X-Road is open-source software and it provides developing countries with a national data exchange infrastructure without licensing fees. By implementing X-Road, countries avoid a vendor lock-in situation and get multiple channels for support, including a global community of users., Different healthcare platforms can be connected securely with X-Road which enables data exchange between private and public service providers. All the evidence regarding the data exchange is stored locally by the data exchange parties, and no third parties have access to the data. Steps are being taken to introduce X-Road on a global basis, to allow either the World Health Organization (WHO) or its member states to set up various cross-border services to help the global community emerge faster from the COVID-19 health and economic crisis., Energy efficiency, renewables and consumer centricity figure among the lines of action to boost the transition towards cleaner energy systems – ways of producing, delivering and consuming energy in a more sustainable way. The deployment of information technology has a significant impact on the feasibility of contemporary policy actions. X-Road is helping electricity grid operators by harmonising access to energy data. By simplifying access to data lets them focus on the solutions to achieve energy and climate goals., X-Road enables reduction of administrative burdens by the implementation of the Once-Only Principle (TOOP). Streamlined administrative processes support economic growth and enable providing better services for the citizens. For example, in Estonia, X-Road saved 1,134 working years during the previous calendar year. X-Road helps a country to become a hassle-free environment for business and entrepreneurship, which also attracts foreign investments., X-Road provides national core digital infrastructure for data exchange between organizations across administration sectors and business domains. Typically, the ecosystem is open for all kinds of organizations – both public and private sector organizations. Besides, X-Road can be used to implement cross-border data exchange with other countries. X-Road enables allocating resources for building digital services and fostering innovation, instead of integrating services point-to-point., The use of digital services reduces the need to travel between different locations which reduces traffic in the cities. When travelling is needed, digital services provide information about different transportation and route alternatives and may prioritise the most environmentally friendly alternatives. X-Road is a crucial enabler that’s needed to make numerous information systems to communicate with each other. By establishing or joining an X-Road environment, cities and municipalities can request up-to-date information from relevant public registers and increase their effectiveness., The Nordic Institute for Interoperability Solutions (NIIS) aims to develop X-Road the most sustainable data exchange solution in the world. The short-term goal is to focus on the X- Road software's direct and tangible environmental impacts. NIIS conducted research focusing on assessing the current emissions profile across X-Road's operations and services to give targeted recommendations for emissions reduction and sustainable business practices., X-Road is a solution to fight against corruption and helps in building trust towards institutions. X-Road provides log records of each message sent between X-Road ecosystem member organisations. The log records provide undeniable evidence of a transaction, and they could be used in process automation to reduce manual work, increase the level of automation in various processes and make things easier for both users of different information systems and citizens. X-Road also provides many features that are required from MyData platform technology.

name: Agrontology
project_description: The Agrontology adds a semantic layer to any agri-food vocabulary (or dataset), providing domain-specific properties for concepts in the areas covered by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Domain-specific semantic relations improve data and information exchange across repositories and institutions, which is essential to make and monitor progress towards the SDGs: in the case of the Agrontology, particularly the SDGs that have indicators for which FAO is the custodian UN agency. FAO is the custodian UN agency for 21 indicators and is a contributing agency to 5 more, spanning SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 12, 14 and 15.

name: Rural Environmental Registry Registration Module
project_description: The Rural Environmental Registry (RER) directly contributes to several Sustainable Development Goals by integrating environmental management with sustainable rural development. Regarding SDG 2 (Zero Hunger and Sustainable Agriculture), RER promotes environmentally responsible agricultural production, encouraging sustainable land use and environmental regularization of rural properties to increase productivity without harming ecosystems (Target 2.4). For SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), RER calculates and identifies Permanent Preservation Areas (PPAs), which are native vegetation areas that should be kept conserved around water bodies of every kind, protecting springs and riparian forests, strengthening watershed management, and ensuring water quality (Target 6.3, 6.5, 6.6). Concerning SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), it may be used to enable access to public policies that support sustainable rural activities, fostering income generation and employment with social and environmental responsibility (Target 8.2, 8.3, 8.4). In SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), RER promotes balanced agricultural practices, restoration of degraded areas, and production traceability, encouraging sustainable consumption and production patterns (Target 12.2). SDG 13 (Climate Action) is the main SDG related to RER. The solution and environmental concepts behind it enable states to share responsibility for forest and environmental conservation with society, namely rural landholders and landowners. The main concept behind RER is that every rural property should play a role in conserving sensitive environmental assets, such as water streams and water springs, and forests located in their area. This allows for deforestation monitoring and reduction, maintenance of carbon stocks, payment for environmental services, protection of water sources, soil and biodiversity, thus reinforcing evidence-based climate policies (Target 13.2). Regarding SDG 14 (Life Below Water), RER protects riverbanks and water springs, helping to reduce pollution and sedimentation that impact aquatic and coastal ecosystems (Target 14.1, 14.2). Finally, in SDG 15 (Life on Land), RER plays a key role in conserving, restoring, and ensuring the sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems by monitoring vegetation cover, promoting forest recovery, and protecting biodiversity (Target 15.2, 15.3, 15.4).

name: KoboToolbox
project_description: SDG 10 & SDG 11 - Humanitarian response and peacebuilding: In Ukraine and neighboring countries, the IFRC and national Red Cross societies are using KoboToolbox to conduct needs assessments and provide critical support to people affected by the conflict. In Niger, KoboToolbox is used to plan and supervise infrastructure investments for refugees, providing improved access to shelter and other crucial resources. In Ukraine, UNHCR is using KoboToolbox to inform emergency response efforts and provide humanitarian assistance, including relocation initiatives and cash-based interventions, in collaboration with local authorities, United Nations agencies, and displaced community groups. WeWorld-GVC, an organization dedicated to supporting development cooperation and humanitarian aid, used KoboToolbox to successfully digitize their fleet management data collection in Burundi. With their improved fleet management system, they have greater access to the data and insights needed for more efficient logistics and more effective crisis response. KoboToolbox was selected as the official data collection and coordination tool for the Recovery and Peacebuilding Process in the Central African Republic. In the aftermath of Hurricane Iota in late 2020, KoboToolbox has been used to streamline data collection and disaster relief efforts in Cartagena, improving access to basic necessities for 5,000 households in affected communities. SDG 13 - Climate change and environmental protection: As part of the World Bank Air Quality Management technical assistance program which aims to reduce air pollution in the Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) states, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) used KoboToolbox to conduct a survey that informed a Clean Cookstove Pilot in Bihar and established 25 women-led energy enterprises in the area. The Climate Smart Agriculture and Water (CSAW Sofala) project in Mozambique aims to improve the livelihoods of 7,800 smallholder farm families in the Sofala province and build resilience to future stressor events. Using KoboToolbox to collect precise geolocation data, the CSAW team is able to make more accurate data-driven decisions and monitor the progress and impact of the project. The Environmental Justice Foundation, an organization dedicated to promoting a sustainable global environment, has been using KoboToolbox to document the nature and scale of illegal fishing and human rights abuses on board the world's largest distant water fishing fleets. Blue Ventures, a marine conservation organization, is using KoboToolbox to support remote and rural coastal communities to monitor fisheries themselves with access to real-time data and insights. Blue Ventures’ work in Madagascar, Indonesia, Timor-Leste, and Comoros shows how KoboToolbox can be used to drive community-led action for change and protect the coastal environment for future generations. SDG 4 - Education: KoboToolbox partnered with Education Above All (EAA) and UNESCO to build the Track Attacks on Education (TRACE) Data Portal. TRACE is an online portal that supports the collection and sharing of accurate real-time data about attacks on education. The portal is crucial to sharing information with affected communities, humanitarian actors, and development workers as well as providing reliable data to inform policy, advocacy, and reporting. To better understand the needs of schools and students and to improve resource distribution, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) Ministry of Education used KoboToolbox to create the first database of all the country’s primary and secondary schools. SDG 5 & SDG 10 - Social and economic development: In the Philippines, the Department of Agrarian Reform uses KoboToolbox to gather crucial geo-tagged data for the Support to Parcelization of Lands for Individual Titling project which aims to build the resilience and resources of local farmers. In Cambodia, KoboToolbox empowers communities to collect and analyze WASH data, giving them increased agency in decision making and resource allocation. In Siem Reap province, HURREDO (Human Resource and Rural Economic Development Organization) helped establish a women-led community-based organization called Run Samaki for Development (RSD), which is focused on addressing key water and sanitation issues in their community. Using KoboToolbox, the Caribbean Development Bank’s Basic Needs Trust Fund (BNTF) is working to build local community capacity and reduce poverty in nine Caribbean countries by promoting economic and social development initiatives that improve quality of life. Data collected with KoboToolbox helps direct BNTF’s grant financing towards sustainable and inclusive development for the most vulnerable communities. KoboToolbox is central to an initiative that is actively engaged in improving labor conditions for workers in the cane sugar supply chain. CNV Internationaal’s Labor Rights Observatory initiative provided a platform for the voices of sugar workers to be heard, with the insights gathered using KoboToolbox leading to the publication of the first annual report for the Latin American sugar cane sector. SDG 3 - Health: To support the health of school children in Uganda, KoboToolbox has been used to monitor crucial deworming activities that ensure their well-being. To improve access to healthcare, KoboToolbox has been used in Sudan to map remote health facilities and track available services and medicine. More stories about how KoboToolbox is being used around the world can be found on our blog: https://www.kobotoolbox.org/blog/

name: National Carbon Credit Registry
project_description: SDG7: Lowering costs of green energy programmes SDG8:Creating green job ecosystem SDG9: Encouraging micro to large-scale green innovation initiatives SDG12: Establishing international green trade technical schemas SDG13: Encouraging faster adoption of carbon credit offsets to reduce greenhouse gasses SDG17: Allowing government ownership as well as private participation in an open marketplace

name: OpenSPP
project_description: OpenSPP enables governments and humanitarian agencies to support the underprivileged through assistance programs. The platform supports both cash transfer and in-kind transfer activities. OpenSPP is currently being deployed in the Middle East to support a country-wide government in-kind transfer program that targets the most vulnerable populations (helping towards the achievement of Target 1.3)., OpenSPP can be used to distribute food assistance to the most vulnerable populations thanks to offline registration and advance targeting of qualified beneficiaries. MUAC monitoring for mother and child can be implemented to distribute specialized nutritious foods to prevent stunting in children under 5 of age (helping towards the achievement of Target 2.2). OpenSPP is currently being deployed in the Middle East to support a country-wide government in-kind transfer program that targets the most vulnerable populations (helping towards the achievement of Target 2.1)., OpenSPP can be used to implement various types of health and well-being programs, from antenatal and postnatal programs to ensure maternal and child well-being to the distribution of health and hygiene kits. For instance, programs can be configured to implement cash or food distribution in the context of MUAC monitoring for mother and child (helping towards the achievement of Targets 3.1 and 3.2)., OpenSPP can be used to implement attendance tracking in school feeding programs that provide both educational and health benefits to the most vulnerable children. School feeding programs act as an incentive for families to enroll and keep children in school (helping towards the achievement of Targets 4.1 and 4.2)., From intent and design to implementation, OpenSPP allows for the integration of gender considerations into all aspects of a social protection program (helping towards the achievement of Target 5.1). The platform can also be used to create and manage school feeding programs that, according to WFP, empower girls by dissuading parents from marrying them off early, which halts their education and can result in child pregnancies., From intent and design to implementation, OpenSPP allows for the integration of inequality considerations into all aspects of a social protection program, helping beneficiaries receive what they need. OpenSPP helps governments implement and monitor social protection policies (helping towards the achievement of Target 10.4)., OpenSPP is developed by people in the Global South (Thailand, the Philippines, Laos, and Vietnam) for the Global South (helping towards the achievement of Targets 17.6 and 17.9), and it allows and encourages local companies to provide support for the solution. OpenSPP is particularly well suited to provide support to developing countries to significantly increase the availability of high-quality, timely and reliable data disaggregated by income, gender, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographic location and other characteristics relevant in national contexts (helping towards the achievement of Target 17.I).

name: QField
project_description: QField's capabilities extend beyond just one aspect of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); they intersect with multiple goals, enhancing efforts towards a sustainable future. SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation): QField supports the mapping and monitoring of water resources, aiding in the management of clean water and sanitation projects. SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure): By promoting innovative data collection methods, QField contributes to building resilient infrastructure and fostering innovation. SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities): Urban planners utilize QField for sustainable urban development, ensuring that cities grow harmoniously with natural resources. SDG 13 (Climate Action): Environmentalists leverage QField to track climate change impacts, helping to inform and implement measures to combat climate change. SDG 14 (Life Below Water): The application aids in the collection of marine data, which is crucial for protecting life below water through sustainable ocean management. SDG 15 (Life on Land): QField is instrumental in biodiversity conservation projects, enabling tracking species and habitats to preserve life on land. SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions): By improving transparency in data collection, QField helps strengthen institutions and supports enforcing laws and policies related to environmental protection. QField is a versatile tool that empowers various stakeholders to contribute to multiple SDGs through improved data accessibility and decision-making processes.

name: NotesMaster
project_description: As a freely accessible elearning platform, NotesMaster provides access to quality lessons in 31 countries, authored by local teachers and based around the local curriculum. The digital content authored on Notesmaster is published under Creative Commons Licenses CC BY SA 4.0 and can be copied and repurposed by all education stakeholders. The OER content can be remixed and easily shared to support diverse curricula. All content on Notesmaster is a digital public good and can be used on the platform or downloaded to MS Word and used away from the platform. It can also be accessed without login for use in other learning platforms. The recent UNICEF-NotesMaster program in Trinidad and Tobago has produced OER content that is being used and reversioned by participants of similar OER programs in Dominica, Grenada, Zambia, Namibia and Malawi., In the OER content programs NotesMaster manages for the Commonwealth of Learning we use the Common Wealth of Learning Gender Mainstreaming Toolkit for Teachers and Teacher Educators as well as the Checklist for the Development of Gender-Responsive Learning Materials to ensure that gender equality is met in all subjects developed., NotesMaster is an online education innovation in that it allows content to be created by local teachers, that is based around the local curriculum. The NotesMaster Library allows the content from all 31 countries to be easily accessed, used or remixed to suit local customs. The library also supports access in other popular learning platforms such as Edmodo, and Google Classroom., Through free and open access to quality education resources for formal learners and also second chance learners. Notesmaster collaborated with its partner the Caribbean Examinations Council to implement the '2nd Chance Program' to the ‘at risk’ youth population (16-30 age group) in 9 regional territories of the Caribbean., Through its partnership with the Namibian College of Open Learning, NotesMaster was pleased to be awarded a WSA for best societal impact for its digital resources. This program led to improved outcomes for communities in Namibia and for second chance learners aged 14-21., Through a collaboration with Commonwealth of Learning, Ministry of Education Zambia, and local teachers, education officers and other partners, NotesMaster successfully piloted eLearning technologies in Muchinga Province, Zambia which in its first year saw an 11% increase (37% to 49%) in pass rates for secondary level exams. Muchinga province moved from 11th (last) on the results charts to 7th. The program is being scaled up in 2021-2022. The link shows the news coverage of the program, with the Provincial Education Officer, praising the achievements.

name: FAOLEX
project_description: The FAOLEX database is relevant for a wide range of SDG goals and targets. It is highly relevant for specific indicators such as: Indicators 5.a.2: Proportion of countries where the legal framework (including customary law) guarantees women’s equal rights to land ownership and/or control Indicator 6.5.1: Degree of integrated water resources management implementation (0-100). Indicator 12.1.1: Number of countries developing, adopting, or implementing policy instruments aimed at supporting the shift to sustainable consumption and production. Indicator 14.6.1: Progress by countries in the degree of implementation of international instruments aiming to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. Indicator 14.b.1: Degree of application of a legal/regulatory/policy/institutional framework which recognizes and protects access rights for small-scale fisheries. Indicator 15.6.1: Number of countries that have adopted legislative, administrative, and policy frameworks to ensure fair and equitable sharing of benefits. Indicator 15.8.1: Proportion of countries adopting relevant national legislation and adequately resourcing the prevention or control of invasive alien species.

name: Dalgo
project_description: Dalgo supports the social sector statistical capacity building in the nonprofits that use it. Our current nonprofit users work in the fields of water quality (SDG 6), early childhood education, K-12 education (SDG 4), vocational education, 21st-century skills (SDG 8), sanitation rights, and child and maternal health (SDG 3). By way of consolidation of intervention data collected from different sources, we enable nonprofits to generate holistic insights on their impact in these fields which inform their practice and communication of their impact. In line with SDG 9 target 9B - Support domestic technology development and industrial diversification: Dalgo also enables nonprofits to bring relevance to public data through the automated ingestion and processing of data from public data sources which is then made conveniently accessible to beneficiaries via on-ground or digital intervention (WhatsApp chatbots/webapps).

name: Green Roads Toolkit
project_description: SDG 6 – Clean Water and Sanitation (Relevant targets: 6.3, 6.6) The Green Roads Toolkit supports early-stage planning and assessment by helping project teams and decision makers identify road design and drainage practices that reduce pollution, manage runoff, and protect water bodies and watersheds, directly contributing to improved water quality and ecosystem protection. SDG 7 – Affordable and Clean Energy (Relevant targets: 7.3) Through planning and option assessment, the toolkit enables the selection of energy-efficient and low-carbon road solutions, helping reduce life-cycle energy consumption in transport infrastructure and supporting improvements in energy efficiency. SDG 11 – Sustainable Cities and Communities (Relevant targets: 11.2, 11.6) The toolkit is used during planning and appraisal to assess how road investments can improve accessibility, safety, and environmental performance, supporting inclusive mobility while reducing pollution and negative urban impacts. SDG 13 – Climate Action (Relevant targets: 13.1, 13.2) By integrating climate risk screening and decarbonization considerations into project planning, the toolkit helps decision-makers prioritize road alignments and designs that reduce greenhouse gas emissions and enhance climate resilience. SDG 15 – Life on Land (Relevant targets: 15.1, 15.5) The toolkit supports planning and environmental assessment processes by guiding the selection of road practices that avoid sensitive habitats, reduce land degradation, and incorporate biodiversity-friendly measures, minimizing impacts on terrestrial ecosystems.

name: Interfacer
project_description: SDG 11 - Sustainable Cities and Communities: The project's emphasis on the Interfacer model and the re-localization of production to urban areas corresponds with SDG 11's objective of creating inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainable cities. By enabling communities to collaboratively produce goods and services, the solution actively contributes to sustainable urban development. SDG 9 - Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure: The adoption of the Interfacer approach and the development of necessary digital infrastructure underscore the significance of innovation and technological advancement in driving circular economies. Through the promotion of open-source practices and global data sharing, the solution supports the advancement of industries and infrastructure in a sustainable manner. SDG 12 - Responsible Consumption and Production: The project's core aim of empowering communities to produce what they consume aligns seamlessly with SDG 12's target of ensuring responsible consumption and production patterns. By advocating for collaborative development and shared data, the solution contributes to minimizing waste and promoting sustainable resource management. SDG 13 - Climate Action: The focus on establishing regenerative urban models and promoting environmentally conscious production methods resonates with SDG 13's mission to combat climate change and its impacts. By endorsing sustainable practices and localized production, the solution plays a role in climate mitigation efforts. SDG 17 - Partnerships for the Goals: The project's collaborative approach in creating the Interfacer model and facilitating global data sharing aligns harmoniously with SDG 17's emphasis on forging partnerships and global cooperation. Through its encouragement of collaboration among communities, governments, and stakeholders, the solution strives to achieve shared sustainability objectives. In summary, the Interfacer team's solution, centered around the Interfacer model, establishes a robust relationship with several key SDGs by addressing urban sustainability, innovation, responsible consumption and production, climate action, and the fostering of partnerships.

name: Aam Digital
project_description: Aam Digital is used by social sector organizations that directly work with beneficiaries on the ground. As a customizable software platform, it is contributing to the work of organizations working towards a number of SDGs: Projects use Aam Digital to track & coordinate - living conditions and interventions to improve livelihoods (SDG 1); - beneficiaries' health status and health-related activities (SDG 3); - student support programs, learning progress, and attendance at educational activities (SDG 4); - work focused on gender equity and girls' rights (SDG 5); - activities of capacity building for SMEs and their outcomes (SDG 8); - work with marginalized communities (SDG 10) - activities to overcome conflict and stereotypes (SDG 16) - with its data management and reporting Aam Digital provides an easy way to evaluate and communicate work between partnerships across the globe with transparency and accountability (SDG 16)

name: WaPOR
project_description: SDG 1: No poverty, SDG2: Zero Hunger,SDG6: Clean Water and Sanitation,SDG13: Climate Action,SDG15: Life on land Answer 2: The project is particularly suited to address and monitor the 6th SDG on water and sanitation, more precisely target 6.4: “by 2030, substantially increase water-use efficiency across all sectors and ensure sustainable withdrawals and supply of freshwater to address water scarcity and substantially reduce the number of people suffering from water scarcity”. WaPOR contributes to achieving the following sustainable development goals: SDG 1: to end poverty in all its forms everywhere, by supporting more resilient agricultural systems that can better and more reliably meet the needs of the people that work and depend on them. SDG 2: to end hunger, achieve food security and improve nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture, by supporting resilient agricultural systems that draw sustainably from available water resources. SDG 6: to ensure the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all, by supporting water management initiatives with robust data that allows informed decision-making as well as supporting solutions that can help water users in agriculture make the most of their share of this dwindling resource, while ensuring that other water users can also get access, including environmental flows. SDG 13: to take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts, by contributing to strengthening of the resilience and adaptive capacity of agricultural systems to climate-related hazards and the unpredictable changes in the weather patterns, SDG 15: to protect, restore and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, and halt and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss, by supporting increases in the productivity of existing cultivated lands, informing water management efforts that do not compromise on the importance of water flows that are essential to certain ecosystems, contributing to the monitoring of land cover, among others. link: https://www.fao.org/in-action/remote-sensing-for-water-productivity/wapor-sdg/en

name: CityLearn
project_description: CityLearn allows to work out how end-use energy demand can be shifted throughout the day. This helps aligning demand with availability of renewable energy resources (solar, wind), which reduces the reliance on fossil fuel powered thermal power generators. A specific problem of reducing cost, emissions and providing grid services has been used in the 2022 CityLearn Challenge here https://www.aicrowd.com/challenges/neurips-2022-citylearn-challenge CityLearn can be generalized to a variety of use cases though. It is the only tool that allows to work out demand-side energy shifting at scale.

name: CodeCarbon
project_description: CodeCarbon allow users to understand how much energy and CO2 emissions are associated with a computer process. Knowing that the user could relocate the process to a region with less carbon-intensive electricity or reduce the electricity consumption with optimisation (Target 12.2, 12.6).

name: Aid Management Platform
project_description: The Aid Management Platform (AMP) aligns with SDG 16's specific target 16.6 of "develop[ing] effective, accountable and transparent institutions at all levels" by providing governments and development partners with a tool that allows for both parties to conduct better resource planning, identify gaps and duplications in foreign assistance, better align foreign assistance to national priorities, and to make information about aid flows more transparent to civil society, citizens, journalists, researchers, and other stakeholders.

name: Eco-Index Biodiversity Dashboards
project_description: In line with SDG Target 15.5: Protect biodiversity and natural habitats, the digital tools that Eco-index creates help users track and understand the health of terrestrial biodiversity over time. This is relevant to all terrestrial ecosystem types (forests, wetlands, etc.). The tool is also being designed for use by local and national governments that are looking to bring their own biodiversity targets.

name: Energy Access Explorer
project_description: Energy services are highly interconnected with socio-economic development and human well-being. Yet, life without reliable energy is a reality for more than 675 million people globally. Effectively expanding energy access requires proper energy planning and access to transparent analytical tools and data. To help address this challenge, WRI, in collaboration with partners has developed the Energy Access Explorer (EAE), a data-driven, integrated and inclusive approach to achieving universal access to energy for equitable, socio-economic development. EAE provides geospatial data and analytics necessary to create a future where all people and institutions have access to affordable, reliable and modern energy (SDG7).

name: Productive Forests
project_description: BIOVERSE was able to identify 5 -20 X more trees than initially known by the Indigenous Community of Kayapo and the Quilombola Community of Cachoeira Porteira. The economic impact of mapping the location of non-timber-related trees and serving the data to the community in the form of abundance maps makes a big difference in the harvesters' earnings potential. Productive Forests initiative directly impacts harvesting logistics and yields and, therefore, improves the lives of non-timber-related forest harvesters., Forest communities have very few options for generating income. Most employment and revenue-generating opportunities are linked to cattle ranching, deforestation, logging, mining, illegal wildlife hunting, and animal trafficking. The Productive Forests initiative seeks to strengthen income generation from sustainable practices such as the harvest of non-timber-related trees species that produce fruits, nuts, sap, and extracts and secures perennial crop harvesting while maintaining the forest standing for subsequent generations.

name: Marine Spatial Planning - SAHAV
project_description: SDG11: SAHAV helps to create sustainable, resilient coastal and marine environments that enhance urban planning and ensure inclusive, safe, and accessible environments for coastal communities. SDG13: SAHAV supports climate action through the sustainable management of marine and coastal ecosystems, which helps mitigate climate change impacts and enhance resilience. SDG14: SAHAV promotes sustainable use and protection of marine resources, conserving marine biodiversity, and preventing over-exploitation of ocean ecosystems. SDG15: SAHAV ensures the conservation and sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems and biodiversity, particularly in coastal and marine areas that are critical for both land and sea ecosystems.

name: Accessible Kazakhstan
project_description: The 'Accessible Kazakhstan' map reflects the needs of those who particularly seek accessible, safe and comfortable public space, including people with disabilities, parents with small children in prams, the elderly, pregnant women, temporarily injured people and children under seven years old. When monitoring a public facility, the owner of the facility is present, and the project team immediately notifies him or her of which elements of the facility do not meet the standards for accessibility of facilities open to the public. On the portal “Accessible Kazakhstan” one can find checklists with criteria for assessing accessibility of facilities, so that, if desired, the owners can read them and afterwards be involved in monitoring independently. Upon request, the project team develops recommendations, on the basis of which owners and government agencies start working on the adaptation of particular facilities for the aforementioned categories of citizens. Based on current data on accessibility of public facilities, comprehensive policies and plans for inclusion can be adopted and implemented. This, in turn, will reduce inequalities and accelerate achievement of other Sustainable Development Goals that affect development of an inclusive society. The world community needs qualified specialists who are able to form a barrier-free environment. It is for the purpose of training such specialists in 2019 within the framework of the “Accessible Kazakhstan” project that a unique online course “Ensuring accessibility of a public facility” was developed. The course: helps to get acquainted with legislation governing the provision of access to public facilities for people with disabilities and other population groups with limited mobility; can be used to find out what criteria accessibility of public facilities and open spaces is evaluated by; explains how to protect one’s right to a barrier-free environment; teaches how to monitor a public facility and develop recommendations for its adaptation to the needs of people with disabilities.

name: AccessMod
project_description: AccessMod contributes to SDG target 3.8: achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by ensuring that all people have a physical access to the health services they need where they need them. It has been used in more than 40 low- and middle-income countries, and also in support of national health authorities and international health programs and organizations (WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF, The Global Fund, The World Bank, IDB, FIND).

name: African Storybook
project_description: The African Storybook is composed of 4269 storybooks and 8098 translations available in 242 languages which provides open access to picture storybooks in the languages of Africa and many others for children’s literacy, enjoyment, and imagination. This is in line with SDG4: Quality Education and its target 4.1 Free primary and secondary education and 4.2 Equal access to quality pre-primary education. There are also reviews and descriptions of African Storybook at: https://www.alllanguageresources.com/african-storybook/ https://allafrica.com/stories/202202110011.html - This review stresses the importance of quality storybooks in indigenous languages which is one of the features of ASb https://oep.merlot.org/docs/african-storybook.pdf A published research article on ASb can be found here: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/modl.12374

name: Altinn
project_description: It’s essential for governments and institutions to be able to have effective dialogue with its population an businesses using a trusted platform. Altinn is such a platform, used by every organisation and the whole population in Norway, since 2003.

name: Android FHIR SDK
project_description: Through this toolkit, we make it easier for developers to build mobile health applications specifically designed to meet the needs of low-resource settings, in particular in LMICs. Through our collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), we also enable the deployment of digitized clinical guidelines (SMART Guidelines) for improving the quality of care. In line with target 3.8 Achieve universal health coverage and 3.C Increase health financing and support health workforce in developing countries.

name: caMicroscope
project_description: The primary use case of caMicroscope is related to SDG Indicator 3.b.2 (Development assistance to medical research & basic healthcare). The caMicroscope platform is designed specifically to enable customizable medical studies for biomedical imaging. This typically takes the form of patholgist studies; for example see https://doi.org/10.1158/1538-7445.AM2022-460 The research itself generally aims to help with SDG Indicator 3.4.1 (Reduce Mortality rate from non-communicable diseases) by focusing on cancer early detection studies.

name: Care | Open Healthcare Network
project_description: Care is an integrated tele-triage+bed allocation+patient shifting+teleICU tool for implementing a decentralised healthcare management strategy. Our goal is to continuously improve the quality and accessibility of healthcare services using digital tools. The tool help states achieve Universal Health Coverage by making healthcare accessible to population closer to home, thereby reducing cost of healthcare and the out-of-pocket expenses borne by the patients. The tool also enables collaborative care delivery between the tertiary and secondary tier through TeleICU solution, improving the overall health outcomes in the peripheries including improving the health outcomes of mother and child, management of communicable and non communicable diseases, allows smaller hospitals to respond better to trauma cases etc. Its pandemic management module also allows early detection of disease outbreaks and aids in better management of capacity and healthcare resources in such regions. CARE exemplifies "SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals" through Target 17.7 and 17.17. CARE is a great example of a sustainable technology available for adoption in developing counties. Moreover through its collaborative model of software development and implementation, the project units developers, students, healthcare professionals, and government bodies. This partnership approach amplifies the impact of healthcare innovations and supports the achievement of targets across multiple SDGs by leveraging collective expertise and resources.

name: Chamilo
project_description: By empowering potential teachers with an easy to use digital tool to provide ubiquitous access to their teaching material to anyone, we allow anyone to share material that will allow other people to learn, self-evaluate and become active contributors of a better world. We also empower the potential teachers to improve their material over time by collecting feedback and editing their content accordingly, which helps provide better quality education. Quality education usually leads (indirectly or directly) to better income, which reduces poverty, improves economic growth, reduces inequalities and allow for better implementation of justice and peace.

name: Cider
project_description: Cider's purpose is to improve the targeting of humanitarian aid and thereby help alleviate poverty, especially the most extreme poverty. Well-targeted aid is an important tool for poverty reduction in pursuit of SDG 1. As an example, Cider informed the Novissi aid program in Togo, which was carried out jointly by the non-profit GiveDirectly, the Togolese government, and the Global Policy Lab at UC Berkeley. Researchers involved found that Cider's poverty predictions were more accurate than predictions we could have obtained using any viable alternative considered, given the time and resource constraints of the program. This increased accuracy enabled funds to be directed to poorer individuals and households. Details of the program, Cider's role in it, and evaluations of effectiveness can be found in Aiken et al (2022), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04484-9.

name: ClimWeb
project_description: SDG: SDG 13: Climate Action - This is the most directly relevant SDG. ClimWeb directly supports climate action by: Enabling early warning systems for climate-related disasters, facilitating climate data sharing and evidence-based decision-making, supporting climate adaptation and mitigation strategies Improving climate resilience through better information delivery.

name: Connect For Life
project_description: Educational health content customized per disease can be shared through the Connect For Life platform with the targeted patient population and this can impact the following SDG targets: SDG 3.3.1: Using the communication from Connect For Life, patients can be stimulated to adhere to their HIV medication intakes and in so doing reduce their risk of transmission to other non-infected individuals. Educational content can also be shared in a discrete fashion to ensure that risks of transmission are known. This educational content can be important for many HIV patient groups such as adolescents, MSM, HIV-infected pregnant women to help prevent transmission to sexual contacts and or to unborn babies. SDG 3.3.2: For TB patients adherence to medication for longer treatment periods is critical to achieve cure. Messages from Connect For Life can take the form of engaging, actionable instructions to help motivate individuals to adhere to therapy and thereby help them to reach care and preventing further transmission.

name: Consul Democracy
project_description: Consul Democracy is used by governments globally on local, regional, and national levels to involve citizens in decision-making, helping to develop effective, accountable, and transparent institutions as well as ensuring responsive, inclusive, participatory, and representative decision-making at all levels. Transparency and accountability are further enhanced thanks to the open-source nature of Consul's development, which is community-based. More on the goals, the way we work and participating institutions can be read at: https://consulfoundation.org/about and https://consulproject.org/ Moreover, we support governments to work on all Sustainable Development Goals with their citizens. We have joined forces with The United Nations Development Programme and the cooperative Enreda to foster participation around the Agenda 2030 by incorporating a SDG module into the software so that entities around the world can use it in their Sustainable Development Goals localization processes.

name: cQube
project_description: Saral can be used across domains for applications that require quick and seamless phygitization of data - capture of physical data in a digital, structured format. This results in significant savings in terms of time and effort that would otherwise be required in order to capture the physical data in a digital format. Sunbird Saral has been successfully used by the state government of the largest state in India (Uttar Pradesh) to conduct state-wide assessments tests for about 17 million students from grade 1 to grade 8 - in order to garner a grassroots level understanding of the learning gaps, as well as the needs and challenges faced by the students. The state had a strong desire to gain a deeper understanding of student performance in order to effectively cater to various programs and student learning needs, which aim to achieve universal foundational literacy and numeracy in primary schools by 2025. However, traditional assessment methods bring forth several challenges - these methods were not at scale or student level, making it difficult to obtain reliable data for the state to make informed decisions. Additionally, the time it took for data to reach the central department from traditional assessment methods was too long, as the process involved physical question paper preparation, exam conduction, answer sheet evaluation, result generation and then manually digitizing results, leading to a delay of up to three to four months. The Saral solution replaces the old answer sheets with OMR-based answer sheets and allows teachers to scan the answer sheet through the Saral App. This process instantly digitizes data and allows the state to receive digitized data on the very same day of scanning. Quick and detailed information provided by Saral Assessments has empowered decision-makers to make data-driven choices and take prompt action to enhance educational outcomes in the state. The state is now also planning for a pilot program to explore the use of Saral for other teacher-led activities such as new student admissions to schools. The app can be used to quickly scan admission forms of students and transfer the data to the state backend systems, resulting in significant saving of time for the teachers.

name: Data Observation Toolkit
project_description: In 2019, the United Nations Statistical Commission stated: “Every misclassified or unrecorded death is a lost opportunity to ensure other mothers and babies do not die in the same way. When it comes to health, better data can be a matter of life and death.” DataKind developed the Data Observation Toolkit (DOT) in response to a gap in digital health solutions space to monitor health data generated by other digital tools for problems with data integrity, quality and other scenarios that might need attention. The toolkit aims to provide easier access to data monitoring without the need for deep technical skills. https://www.datakind.org/2022/02/10/empowering-health-workers-and-community-health-systems/, https://podcasters.spotify.com/pod/show/medxtekafrica/episodes/Ep19---Harnessing-the-power-of-data-science-in-healthcare-e1iijkm, https://medic.org/stories/on-the-road-to-precision-community-health/

name: Decidim
project_description: SDG10: Citizen participation mechanisms are traditionally held in person. Providing a digital channel for participation enables people who are home-bound, people who are busy at work when participatory events happen, or people who are otherwise unable to attend, to take part in participatory processes as well. SDG16: In order for participatory democracy processes to be legitimate, they need to be transparent and audited. Decidim provides transparency to each decision taken within a participatory process by making every vote, discussion, proposal and participation, open and published, so that a digital archive of the process remains for any needed audits. Decidim has also worked to implement traceability mechanisms against tampering which are reflected in Decidim's social contract: https://docs.decidim.org/en/develop/understand/social-contract#_transparency_traceability_and_integrity

name: Deon
project_description: The checklist has explicit items to identify and mitigate biases (relevant to SDG 10). See here for particular items on identifying bias and reducing inequalities (SDG10): https://deon.drivendata.org/#c-analysis

name: DiCRA
project_description: The objective of the DiCRA platform is to provide free and open access to geospatial datasets through an open digital platform thereby enabling concrete evidence-driven policies and concerted action from all stakeholders involved in sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture. Through geospatial analysis and data-powered positive deviance approaches, the platform informs stakeholders on which farms are more resilient to extreme weather events. Indigenous knowledge is tapped through field validation and ethnography to suggest good practices on climate-resilient farming that are already working well through bottom-up approaches, to feed into large-scale agriculture programs and policies and optimize public investments in climate-resilient agriculture. DiCRA platform, therefore, contributes to SDG 2 to 'End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture'. Specifically, DiCRA contributes to SDG target 2.4 which states 'By 2030, ensure sustainable food production systems and implement resilient agricultural practices that increase productivity and production, that help maintain ecosystems, that strengthen capacity for adaptation to climate change, extreme weather, drought, flooding, and other disasters and that progressively improve land and soil quality. , DiCRA platform contributes to SDG 13 'Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts'. With its objective to enhance climate adaptation measures through data-driven approaches as well as the impact on policies for climate resilient agriculture, the DiCRA platform contributes directly to SDG target 13.1 'Strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity to climate-related hazards and natural disasters in all countries' and SDG target 13.2 to 'Integrate climate change measures into national policies, strategies and planning'.

name: Element
project_description: Target 9.1 Develop quality, reliable, sustainable and resilient infrastructure: Element supports the development of resilient digital communication infrastructure by enabling organisations to build sovereign, interoperable, and secure communication systems based on the Matrix open standard. Unlike centralised proprietary platforms, Matrix allows independent servers to interoperate, ensuring communication can continue even during outages, disruptions, or jurisdictional constraints. This creates a more resilient and robust communication layer for organisations, governments, and critical services. Target 9.5 Enhance research and upgrade industrial technologies: Element contributes to technological innovation by building on and actively contributing to the Matrix open standard, including core server components and software development kits within the ecosystem. Matrix is a decentralised protocol for secure real-time communication that enables continuous development of open-source technologies for messaging, collaboration, voice, and video across sectors. Through Matrix, Element promotes open standards and interoperability, enabling seamless communication between providers and reducing fragmentation across public and private systems. This supports a more open, competitive, and innovative digital ecosystem. Element also strengthens secure digital infrastructure through end-to-end encryption, identity verification, and flexible deployment models, including self-hosting. By combining openness, federation, interoperability, and security, Element supports resilient and scalable digital infrastructure aligned with SDG 9. Target 9.b Support domestic technology development and industrial diversification: Element enables organisations and governments to build and operate sovereign communication infrastructure using open-source software and open standards, without dependence on proprietary vendors. Because it is based on Matrix, it supports deployment, modification, and extension by any organisation, protecting against vendor lock-in. This promotes digital sovereignty, strengthens domestic technical expertise, and supports diversified and independent digital infrastructure across regions and sectors, while also encouraging ecosystem competition and reducing reliance on centralised technology providers.

name: epiCo
project_description: epiCo is a package that streamlines analyses commonly performed in ministries of health for the surveillance of vector-borne diseases. It makes these analyses more robust and more automated, thus increasing verifiability and scalability. It has been developed in consultation with the Secretary of Health of Tolima, Colombia.

name: Everwell Hub
project_description: Everwell Hub is a scalable user-centric technology product that can positively impact health with the vision of creating a world where every person is empowered to lead a healthy life. We ensure that all personas in any healthcare setting, be it a health care professional, patient or individual caregiver are kept engaged and enthusiastic about their association with the domain. The product is designed and developed to enable deployments that are easy to use, localized, contextual, configurable, interoperable, secure and is a low-cost digital health solution for both providers as well as care seekers.

name: FAO Global Administrative Unit Layers
project_description: GAUL supports the selected SDG by providing a common unified coding systems for monitoring and visualization relevant indicators into a unified common system. The dataset empowers governments, NGOs, and researchers to act locally while thinking globally. By enabling granular, location-specific insights, it drives more equitable, sustainable, and effective responses to poverty, hunger, environmental degradation, and unsustainable production—directly supporting SDGs 1, 2, 12, and 15.

name: Fedora Linux
project_description: Free access to our open source technology and community provides industry connections and the ability to learn best practices in an established technology project. Community members learn real skills that are relevant in the global job market. Our project mission is directly aligned: Fedora creates an innovative platform for hardware, clouds, and containers that enables software developers and community members to build tailored solutions for their users.

name: Food Fortification Quality Management System
project_description: The Food Fortification Quality Management System (FFQMS) plays a pivotal role in addressing malnutrition by ensuring the quality and traceability of fortified foods, directly supporting Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger). Through its comprehensive quality assurance (QA), quality control (QC), and traceability features, the FFQMS ensures that fortified foods meet essential micronutrient standards like Iron, Folic Acid (B9), and Vitamin B12, etc. Aligning with SDG Target 2.2, which aims to eliminate malnutrition by 2030, the FFQMS strengthens fortification processes to fill crucial micro nutritional gaps. Its traceability mechanisms track the journey of raw materials and fortified products from procurement to distribution, ensuring transparency, safety, and accountability across the supply chain. Additionally, the customization feature of FFQMS's validation protocols ensure that fortified foods consistently deliver the required micronutrients, directly contributing to improving public health outcomes. By supporting large-scale food fortification programs, the FFQMS enhances efforts to combat malnutrition and ensures that vulnerable populations receive nutritionally adequate food. In this way, the system plays a critical role in advancing global efforts to end hunger and achieve sustainable food security for all.

name: Food Price Monitoring and Analysis Tool
project_description: The Food Price Monitoring and Analysis (FPMA) tool directly supports SDG 2: Zero Hunger, specifically Target 2.C, which aims to limit extreme food price volatility and ensure proper functioning of food commodity markets. FPMA leverages the Indicator for Price Anomalies (IPA) to monitor and detect unusual deviations in food prices, providing timely and reliable information to policymakers.
